title: Greedy Best-First in SF: Rushes to the Goal ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First Search sprint toward the destination using only a heuristic estimate. Then see exactly how it can fail when the closest-looking route hides a longer dead-end.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — Why Greedy Best-First Search rushes toward destinations and when it fails ⚡

In this SF (SoMa) map visualization, each grid node is expanded by *only* the heuristic h(n) = estimated distance to the goal (no g(n) cost-so-far like A*).

✅ What you’ll see:
• Greedy picks the “best-looking” frontier node first (lowest h).
• It often finds a fast-looking path early.

⚠️ Why it fails:
• It can get trapped by locally promising shortcuts.
• If the heuristic is misleading (e.g., obstacles create hidden detours), it may backtrack a lot or return a longer path.

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First is a heuristic-driven sprint; A* is a goal-seeking strategist that balances progress + remaining distance.

Debate question: In your experience, would you rather deploy “fast heuristic guesses” (Greedy) or “safer optimal planning” (A*)?

yt_description:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — Why Greedy Best-First Search rushes toward destinations and when it fails ⚡

In this real-world city pathfinding visualization (San Francisco, SoMa), we compare how Greedy Best-First Search uses heuristic pathfinding (h(n) only) to pick the next node—while A* balances g(n) + h(n).

Mechanics (what’s happening in the animation):
• Greedy Best-First expands the frontier node with the lowest estimated distance to the goal.
• Because it ignores cost-so-far, it can get stuck in locally attractive dead-ends.
• When the heuristic is misleading (obstacles hide detours), greedy vs a star diverges.
